title: A decade after Stardew Valley, Eric Barone is still going it alone
excerpt: 10 years after Stardew Valley reinvented “cosy gaming” all by himself, creator Eric Barone tells GQ about the pressures of making its long-awaited follow-up, Haunted Chocolatier
content_html:
Playing in bands as a teen, Eric Barone’s musical endeavours rarely went further than letting rip with his guitar in half-empty bars. After years of enduring polite applause in various nu-metal outfits, however, Barone threw in the towel and took up computer science instead at the University of Washington Tacoma. Decades later, I’m sat front and centre at a sold-out Hammersmith Apollo where the music he composed for his DIY farming sim Stardew Valley is being played by a 35-piece orchestra in celebration of the game’s 10th anniversary. “There's a certain scrappiness to the indie music scene that I think is analogous to the Indie Game Dev scene,” reflects Barone. “Especially Stardew Valley… it's an absolutely unprofessional operation.”

Stardew Valley had a particularly unlikely origin story. A one-man operation, it was built pixel by pixel over four and a half years in a cramped Seattle apartment. Feeling no love for the 2010s dirge of increasingly complex first-person shooters, Barone yearned to create a more wholesome virtual world instead – coding a sprite-led continuation of his favourite childhood escape, SNES farming sim Harvest Moon. With almost no game development experience and zero income to his name, he figured out game creation on the fly, while his patient partner, Amber, supported him financially. “It was just my dumb little project,” explains Barone. “My main goal was just to get better at programming and to have something to work on when I couldn’t find a job.”

Credited as the first “cosy game” – a genre built around non-violent, wholesome play – 2016’s Stardew Valley became Gen Z’s answer to The Sims, shifting over 50 million copies in the process and over 573,4000 monthly Spotify streams for its lo-fi jingling soundtrack. Yet where countless other indie titles of the era have fallen out of favour, Stardew Valley has only gone from strength to strength, still regularly hitting over 100,000 concurrent Steam players a decade on. “It's kind of hard to fathom just how many people have played it, and the impact it's had,” reflects Barone. “It was not part of the plan.”

As Barone toils away at home on his long-awaited follow-up, The Haunted Chocolatier, the pressure is on. Already over four years in the making, Barone had all the time in the world to make Stardew Valley. Now he finds himself facing his own difficult second album – and those visions of half-empty Seattle bars come flooding back. “I've been struggling with that,” admits Barone, “because I really want to recapture that feeling that I had when I was making Stardew Valley. Back then, there was no audience, there was no precedent. Everyone's watching me, and if I don't do things a certain way, it might disappoint millions of people.”

Despite earning millions from Stardew, Barone still insists on keeping its follow-up's development an entirely DIY endeavour, only working with external teams for marketing and to help with coding Stardew’s multiplayer. Name-checking David Lynch as one of his inspirations, Barone believes that there’s a certain artistic purity to creating in isolation. And so Barone is yet to let anyone touch his forthcoming creation – not even Amber. “No one's playing the game until I'm ready to show it,” Barone declares. “If you have a turkey in the oven. You're not going to pull it out halfway and have the guests taste it, right? It needs to be done.”

Thankfully, he's happy to at least talk about his new creation, which transports players to a more “metaphysical” locale. “It is still what I call a town game,” explains Barone of The Haunted Chocolatier, “But it’s more of an action RPG – the main focus is more about adventuring, finding equipment and getting more powerful. There are monsters, there are boss fights. It's for the people in Stardew Valley that go into the mines. That's what I do, honestly.”

First announced in 2021, The Haunted Chocolatier's development is already ekeing towards GTA 6 territory – Barone’s most recent blog post under his “Concerned Ape” alias began with a mea culpa: “Sorry it’s taking so long”. Unlike Barone, many creators of indie game phenomena have chosen anonymity in the hope of distancing themselves from the same anxieties. Vampire Survivors dev Luca Galante, for example, sent his publisher to collect his 2023 BAFTA award on his behalf, avoiding public appearances, while Balatro developer Localthunk has managed to conceal his real name entirely. Turning down in-game collaborations with more established franchises (Eric’s lips are sealed on what those were), Barone has only really leveraged his minor celebrity status a few times: to direct a music video for cult indie-pop band Alvvays and to meet his idol Harvest Moon creator Yasuhiro Wada, who signed his Super Nintendo game cartridge.

Now that he’s done with a run of shows spanning from Colorado’s legendary Red Rocks amphitheatre to Paris’ Bataclan theatre, Barone has returned to isolation in the hope of finishing The Haunted Chocolatier – while being under no illusion that he’ll replicate Stardew Valley’s “once in a generation” kind of unifying success.

At the Hammersmith Apollo, a man proposes to his girlfriend to rapturous applause. It’s an infectiously good-natured crowd, many of whom are dressed in elaborate, colourful cosplay. With chicken plushies clutched in hands, I spot attendees draped in everything from your classic farmer dungarees and straw hats to more bespoke character tributes – including more than a few purple wigs honouring Pelican Town’s resident emo, Abigail.

“I think more than ever, we need unifying, peaceful and joyful media that allows people an escape,” says Barone. “Each element of these games is actually pretty amateur. It's really just a matter of having the willpower to stick with them long enough. I guess that was my main talent.”

Stardew Valley is available now on all major platforms. At stardewvalley.net
